description: HemoScope is a one-person team led by Julianne Chang, a sophomore at the Illinois Mathematics and Science Academy (IMSA). Julianne is passionate about where biology, bioinformatics, and machine learning/AI meet.
summary: On a mission to Mars, help is up to 22 minutes away by radio and months away in person. Astronauts have to notice changes in their own health and decide what to do, with no doctor in the room. HemoScope is offline health monitoring software that gives them a personal early warning system. Instead of comparing astronauts to population ranges built from people on Earth, HemoScope learns each astronaut’s own preflight standard from real blood data and adjusts its expectations for each phase of spaceflight. A Daily Check of vitals, sleep and symptoms and a Blood Check of immune cells become one clear status, backed by the data and trends behind it. Two machine learning models, trained on 1,286 real blood counts and tested on people they had never seen, forecast each astronaut’s next blood check and map their immune state. The Learning Dashboard, offline search chatbot, and an Emergency Mode help crews understand and act on their health, and a private Mind space with a mood journal, guided breathing and short activities helps them look after their wellbeing on long, isolated missions. Everything runs on the device with no internet.

Benefits and intended impact

HemoScope catches health changes that are unusual for one specific astronaut, even when the values still look normal on a standard lab report. It explains every result in plain language, works with no connection to Earth, and gives flight surgeons a crew-wide view. It is built for lunar and Mars missions, where communication delays mean crews must recognize and respond to health changes themselves. The same approach could help people in other remote settings, such as Antarctic research stations, where the nearest doctor may be days away.

Features of HemoScope

HemoScope has two views: one for Astronauts and one for the Flight Surgeon.

Astronaut View

  • Astronauts log a Daily Check (temperature, heart rate, breathing rate, oxygen, blood pressure, sleep, mood and symptoms).
  • Astronauts also log a Blood Check (a complete blood count of five white cell types, with the neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio).
  • HemoScope analyzes the data (see analysis section) and then returns one status which includes Normal for You, Monitor Closely, Contact Flight Surgeon, Contact Flight Surgeon Now and Retake the Sample when the data looks like a measurement error.
  • A main dashboard has a score timeline, check-in streaks and a daily checklist to make it simple for astronauts.
  • A health history tab is where astronauts can view their trend charts, look at their immune scores, forecast ranges, and export their data.
  • The Learn Dashboard teaches astronauts how spaceflight affects their body and what their own numbers mean, through an interactive body map, a mission timeline and explanations.
  • Ask HemoScope, an offline search bot that instantly finds answers in HemoScope’s own lessons and guides.
  • Emergency Mode, with step-by-step guides for four microgravity emergencies and a CPR compression pacer.

Flight Surgeon View

  • A surgeon on Earth or on board can click through every crew member’s status and history.
  • Alerts the flight surgeon to astronauts who need immediate attention

Mental health and wellbeing

  • Long missions are isolating, and crews need a way to look after their minds as well as their bodies. HemoScope gives each astronaut a private wellbeing space.
  • Mood Journal: a daily mood rating from 1 to 5 with optional personal notes.
  • Box Breathing: a guided one-minute breathing exercise to settle stress and refocus.
  • Private Badges: rewards for steady check-ins and calm moments, not for health results.
  • Privacy by design: wellbeing entries are never shown to the flight surgeon, never analyzed, and never change a status. HemoScope supports mental health without turning it into surveillance.

How HemoScope analyzes health data

  • Personal baseline: preflight blood counts set each astronaut’s standard range.
  • Spaceflight adjustment: expected values shift by mission phase (early flight, days 1 to 14; long flight, day 15+), based on published spaceflight immunology research.
  • Vitals scoring: an adapted NEWS2 early warning score with spaceflight changes. Blood pressure expectations rise in flight, and temperature is compared with the astronaut’s own recent in-flight average.
  • Immune Deviation Score: (under blood check history) HemoScope’s own 0 to 100 statistic, which combines how far four white cell types have moved from the astronaut’s standard, scaled by how much each one usually varies within a person.

Machine learning

Both models were trained on both models use 1,286 complete blood counts from 120 healthy adults (NIH ImmPort): 70% of the people were used for training and the other 30% were held out for testing. Training ran on Microsoft Azure Machine Learning, with test results tracked in MLflow and both models registered in Azure. The finished models run in the browser with no internet, and automated tests confirm the app’s numbers match the training code exactly.

  • Next Blood Check Forecast
    • Purpose: predicts the range each white cell count should fall in at the next blood check
    • How it works: a Kalman filter for each marker learns two things from real data: how much that marker naturally drifts over time, and how noisy single measurements are. It then predicts the next value adjusted for the mission phase.
    • Validity: across 1,420 forecasts for 36 unseen people, 96.1% of the real next values fell inside the predicted range (target 95%).
    • Purpose: shows the whole immune picture at once and draws each astronaut’s mission as a path, so slow drifts in score become visible.
    • How it works: PCA compresses the four cell types into two readable axes, Overall Immune Cell Level and Neutrophil-Lymphocyte Balance. A Gaussian mixture model then learns where healthy blood checks fall and divides the map into Very Common, Common, Uncommon and Rare zones.
    • Validity: the 50%, 90% and 99% zones held 51.2%, 92.0% and 99.7% of unseen checks, close to their targets.

Novelty and creativity

  • Each astronaut’s own standard, not Earth’s. Most health tools compare people to population ranges. HemoScope treats every astronaut as their own reference, which catches changes a standard lab report would miss.
  • Spaceflight-aware expectations. The “expected” health metric changes with the phase of the mission based on published spaceflight research.
  • An original statistic. The Immune Deviation Score turns four cell counts into one number that measures how unusual today is for this person.
  • Wellbeing without surveillance. Crews on long missions need a space that is just theirs. HemoScope’s mood journal and breathing tools are private by design, so astronauts can check in with themselves without being monitored.
  • Motivation without pressure. Daily logging works if crews keep doing it on long missions. HemoScope’s private badges reward consistency and self-care, never health numbers, so no astronaut feels judged for being sick or stressed.
  • Monitoring that teaches. HemoScope doesn’t just send alerts; it explains what each number means, so astronauts build their own health knowledge on long missions.

Data Used

  • NASA OSDR OSD-569 - the Inspiration4 complete blood counts.
    • Used as the personal baselines for HemoScope’s demo astronauts.
    • Used to test the Immune State Map model.
    • Used to train and test both machine learning models.
    • Used to measure how much each white cell type normally varies within one healthy person, which the Immune Deviation Score needs.
    • Spaceflight immunology studies (Crucian 2015; Stratis 2023) for the mission-phase adjustments.
    • Spaceflight physiology studies (Norsk 2015; Stahn 2017) for the blood pressure and temperature changes.
    • Biological variation research for each marker’s normal personal range, NEWS2 for vitals scoring, and CTCAE v5 for the hard safety limits.

Tools

TypeScript, Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS 4, SVG charts and Vitest (149 tests) for the app; Python and R for data preparation and model training; Microsoft Azure Machine Learning to train, track (MLflow) and register both models; Vercel for hosting; Framer for the public website.

Notice

Claude was used as a coding and writing assistant. All data, methods and design choices were made by the team, and all AI-assisted code was reviewed and tested. HemoScope itself uses no generative AI.
